notes.text: First day — This was the feast of trumpets, which is called a sabbath, and on which they were to have an holy convocation, Lev. xxiii, 24. And it was on this day, the altar was set up, after their return from captivity; in remembrance of which they had probably kept it ever since, with more than ordinary solemnity.

glossa.text:
*And the seventh month had come. ((BEDA, in Esdr., lib. III, cap. 26, tom. II.))* Which was not far off. For since the wall was finished on the five and twentieth day of the sixth month, only five days remained to the beginning of the seventh month, which from the first day unto the two and twentieth was wholly consecrated with the lawful ceremonies, and when these had been duly celebrated, he then returned, with the princes and the people, to the appointing of the dwellers of the city.

*And all the people was gathered together as one man unto the street which,* etc. ((BED., ibid.)) The devotion of the people and their concord are to be noted, etc., *as far as* by whose singing the people, amid the prayers and the victims, might be more ardently stirred up to the remembrance of the law.

Mystically also, when the city has been built, the divine reading must follow, and the trumpets must sound more frequently, so that the people, initiated into the heavenly sacraments, may be instructed also by the sacred words, and from that time more skilfully, how it ought to live.

*Before the water gate. ((ID., ibid.))* I think that the water gate is said to be in the court of the priests, etc., *as far as* well therefore was the people gathered before the water gate, as being about to be given to drink spiritually of the streams of the Scriptures through its own prelate.

notes.text: The heavens — They are as a legible book, wherein he that runs may read it. The glory - His eternal power and Godhead, his infinite wisdom and goodness. Firmament - Or, the expansion, all the vast space extended from the earth to the highest heavens, with all its goodly furniture.

Day — Every day and night repeats these demonstrations of God's glory. Uttereth - Or, poureth forth, constantly and abundantly, as a fountain doth water; So this Hebrew word signifies. Knowledge - Gives us a clear knowledge or discovery of God their author.

Heard — Or, understood; there are divers nations in the world, which have several languages, so that one cannot discourse with, or be understood by another, but the heavens are such an universal teacher, that they can speak to all people, and be clearly understood by all.

Line — Their lines, the singular number being put for the plural. And this expression is very proper, because the heavens do not teach men audibly, or by speaking to their ears, but visibly by propounding things to their eyes, which is done in lines or writings. Gone - Is spread abroad. Earth - So as to be seen and read, by all the inhabitants of the earth. Words - Their magnificent structure, their exquisite order, and most regular course, by which they declare their author, no less than men discover their minds by their words. Sun - Which being the most illustrious and useful of all the heavenly bodies, is here particularly mentioned.

Bridegroom — Gloriously adorned with light as with a beautiful garment, and smiling upon the world with a pleasant countenance. Chamber - In which he is poetically supposed to have rested all night, and thence to break forth as it were on a sudden. Strong man - Conscious and confident of his own strength.
The ends — His course is constant from east to west, and thence to the east again. So that there is no part of the earth which doth not one time or other feel the benefit of his light and heat.

The law — The doctrine delivered to his church, whether by Moses, or by other prophets. Having discoursed hitherto of the glory of God shining forth in, the visible heavens, he now proceeds to another demonstration of God's glory, which he compares with and prefers before the former. Perfect - Completely discovering both the nature and will of God, and the whole duty of man, what he is to believe and practice, and whatsoever is necessary to his present and eternal happiness. Whereas the creation, although it did declare so much of God, as left all men without excuse, yet did not fully manifest the will of God, nor bring men to eternal salvation. Converting - From sin to God, from whom all men are naturally revolted. Testimony - His law, so called because it is a witness between God and man, what God requires of man, and what upon the performance of that condition, he will do for man. Sure - Hebrew. faithful or true, which is most necessary in a witness: it will not mislead any man, but will infallibly bring him to happiness. Simple - Even persons of the lowest capacities.

Right — Both in themselves, and in their effect, as guiding men in the ready way to eternal happiness. Rejoicing - By the discoveries of God's love to sinful men, in offers and promises of mercy. Commandment - All his commands. Pure - Without the least mixture of error. The eyes - Of the mind, with a compleat manifestation of God's will and man's duty: both which, the works of nature, and all the writings of men discover but darkly and imperfectly.

The fear — The law and word of God, because it is both the object and the rule, and the cause of holy fear. Clean - Sincere, not adulterated with any mixture. Constant and unchangeable, the same for substance in all ages. Judgments - God's laws are frequently called his judgments, because they are the declarations of his righteous will, and as it were his judicial sentence by which he expects that men should govern themselves, and by which he will judge them at the last day.

Who — Thy law, O Lord, is holy and just and good. But I fall infinitely short of it. Cleanse - Both by justification, through the blood of thy son; and by sanctification thro' thy Holy Spirit. Though the first may seem to be principally intended, because he speaks of his past sins. Secret - From the guilt of such sins as were secret either, from others; such as none knows but God and my own conscience: or, from myself; such as I never observed, or did not discern the evil of. Pardon my unknown sins, of which I never repented particularly, as I should have done.

Presumptuous — From known and evident sins, such as are committed against knowledge, against the checks of conscience, and the motions of God's spirit. Dominion - If I be at any time tempted to such sins, Lord let them not prevail over me, and if I do fall into them, let me speedily rise again.

Let — Having prayed that God would keep him from sinful actions, he now prays that God would govern, and sanctify his words and thoughts: and this was necessary to preserve him from presumptuous sins, which have their first rise in the thoughts. Redeemer - This expression seems to be added emphatically, and with special respect to Christ, to whom alone this word Goel can properly belong. A prayer for the king, ver. 1-4. The king and the people rejoice in God, and pray for his help, ver. 5-9. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The heavens shew forth. ((Ibid.))* First, speaking of the incarnation, he commends the preaching of the new law. ((AUG.)) The heavens, the apostles, concerning the glory of Christ in which he is equal to the Father. ((CASS.)) Or the heavens, they who sent the star. *The glory. ((Ibid.))*: That God freely forgives sins. *The works.* ((AUG.)) Those which are according to man, etc., *as far as* and these same are made night to him, giving to the darkened the knowledge which is of things human. ((CASS.)) And this so wonderfully, that it is in all tongues; and so widely, that it is in every part of the compass of the earth.

*Day unto day.* ((CASS.)) He treats of it by demonstration. ((AUG.)) *Day unto day.* The Spirit brings forth to spiritual men the fullness of wisdom, etc., *as far as* this teaching is continued by days and by nights down to those who come after.

*Speeches.* ((CASS.)) Public persuadings. *Words.* Common narrations. *Whose voices are not heard.* He would say more plainly, in whom their voices are not heard, or, the voices of all their words are heard: he does the same thing by means of the relative.

((AUG.)) The Spirit made the first men speak with all tongues, he who was to gather all nations into one; then one man was for all, so now one Christ, head and body.

*In the sun* ((CASS.)) What he praises others for having done, he himself does: he preaches the incarnation. Or in the sun, in the open sight of the world, or in labour. The sun burns, and shines, and varies the seasons. *His tabernacle.* ((AUG.)) As it were a soldier's dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to storm the errors of the world. Or the tabernacle, the Church in the open, not in secret, so as to lie hid. *A bridegroom.* ((CASS.)) So often promised by the prophets, a great likeness of the sacrament: therefore born of a virgin, that he might join to himself the Church a virgin. *Out of his bride-chamber.* ((AUG.)) That is, the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Behold, humble in mercy, but strong in majesty. *As a giant to run.* ((CASS.)) Unshaken, not to be called back, overcoming human nature by his power. *From the highest.* Here the Trinity is shewn, etc., *as far as* it marks the unity of the Trinity. *Neither is there any that can hide himself,* etc. ((AUG.)) The Word made flesh permitted no man to excuse himself out of the shadow of death: because the heat of the Word pierced even that. Or, the heat is the Spirit, whom he sent when he had returned, who is law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear and judgments, because he does these things.

*The law of the Lord.* ((CAS.)) Secondly, he praises the precepts of the New and the Old Testament. ((Ibid.)) The law given through Moses, correcting all things by the distinction of its words, and sending them on to the grace of Christ. *Converting.* ((AUG.)) By liberty, unto the imitating of himself, not pressing down with the yoke of servitude. *Souls.* Wills, not merely hands, as the Old Testament did. *The testimony.* Whatsoever *Quaecunquae* testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and have given wisdom to the humble. *Wisdom:* concerning things divine.

*The justices of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* All are right in him, who taught not what he did not do, so that they who imitate them might rejoice in them, seeing they would do them freely with charity, not slavishly with fear. ((CASS.)) *Justices,* the law which justifies; whatsoever it commands is just.

*The fear of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not profitable, and it changes with the times. *The fear of the Lord* is without any perturbation, because it is a love mingled with dread, because if it fears the judge, it knows him merciful. ((AUG.)) Fear, not that penal fear for earthly things, for love of which the soul is afraid, but the chaste fear whereby, the more it loves, the more it is wary of offending the bridegroom, and therefore it is not cast out, but abides. *Judgments.* The judgments of God need not another's authority.

*Desirable things. ((Ibid.))* Or, much to be desired, or much gold and stone; or much that is precious. Desirable above gold, etc., *as far as,* whose will he sets before his own, and they are sweeter than he himself is to himself. *Above gold,* that is, everything that is sought after, whether for riches, or for power, or for pleasure. *Honey.* The food of God is honey; that is, one now loosed from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, because he is still wrapped about, for whom there is need of the pressure of God's hand squeezing him out, that he may go into life.

*Who understandeth sins. ((Ibid.))* Thirdly he asks to be purged of vices, that he may be a worthy psalmist, to report these sacraments. To a mind that sees, truth is sweet, and judgments sweet; to one that does not see, what sweetness is there? But why is it not seen? Because of sins: nor is it any wonder: *For who understandeth sins?* ((CASS.)) *Sins:* all of them, for certain of them are known. *Mine* defile, *others'* afflict, and now spare, drive back the persuader. *From my secret ones.* He includes all sins under two heads, etc., *as far as* whereby man was seduced; and by consenting he made it his own. ((AUG.)) There is no greater sin than to apostatize from God, which is the beginning of pride: but pride is the beginning and the cause of all sin.

notes.text: So is Christ — That is, the body of Christ, the church.

For by that one Spirit, which we received in baptism, we are all united in one body. Whether Jews or gentiles — Who are at the greatest distance from each other by nature. Whether slaves or freemen - Who are at the greatest distance by law and custom. We have all drank of one Spirit - In that cup, received by faith, we all imbibed one Spirit, who first inspired, and still preserves, the life of God in our souls.

The foot is elegantly introduced as speaking of the hand; the ear, of the eye; each, of a part that has some resemblance to it. So among men each is apt to compare himself with those whose gifts some way resemble his own, rather than with those who are at a distance, either above or beneath him. Is it therefore not of the body — Is the inference good? Perhaps the foot may represent private Christians; the hand, officers in the church; the eye, teachers; the ear, hearers.
The ear — A less noble part. The eye - The most noble.
As it hath pleased him — With the most exquisite wisdom and goodness.
But one body — And it is a necessary consequence of this unity, that the several members need one another.
Nor the head — The highest part of all. To the foot - The very lowest.
The members which appear to be weaker — Being of a more delicate and tender structure; perhaps the brains and bowels, or the veins, arteries, and other minute channels in the body.
We surround with more abundant honour — By so carefully covering them. More abundant comeliness - By the help of dress.
Giving more abundant honour to that which lacked — As being cared for and served by the noblest parts.
Now ye — Corinthians. Are the body and members of Christ - part of them, I mean, not the whole body.

First apostles — Who plant the gospel in the heathen nations. Secondly prophets - Who either foretel things to come, or speak by extra-ordinary inspiration, for the edification of the church. Thirdly teachers - Who precede even those that work miracles. Under prophets and teachers are comprised evangelists and pastors, Eph. iv, 11. Helps, governments - It does not appear that these mean distinct offices: rather, any persons might be called helps, from a peculiar dexterity in helping the distressed; and governments, from a peculiar talent for governing or presiding in assemblies.

Ye covet earnestly the best gifts — And they are worth your pursuit, though but few of you can attain them. But there is a far more excellent gift than all these; and one which all may, yea, must attain or perish. The necessity of love is shown, ver. 1-3. The nature and properties, ver. 4-7. The duration of it, ver. 8-13 Verse

glossa.text: *So also Christ.* Christ is called head and body, on account of the ineffable unity of the head and of the members. One spirit will do all things in the members of the body of Christ, as one soul sees in the eye, hears in the ear, and in all the rest does all things.

*For indeed.* He shows how the body of Christ is one, because we have all been baptized, that is, washed, and led in one spirit unto this, that we may be one body, that is, of one mind through that one spirit, as the whole body of a man is quickened by one soul. And because we have all been given to drink in the receiving of the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit, *in one spirit:* because he directs all the gifts to the effecting of one thing. That man's person is not to be contemned or preferred, nor is the glory of God to be given to men: because one and the same works in all.

*For the body also.* He shows by the similitude of the human body that the unity of the body of Christ, that is, of the Church, has variety of offices, and that this diversity does not take away unity: as the unity of the human body consists not in singleness, but in many members, that they may render to one another what they owe.
*If the whole.* As if he should say: If in the Church all were of one office, how would the need of the body be fulfilled, for whose governance divers things are needful?.

*Members, every one of them as he would.* *Memora*; read *membra*, "members" (I Cor. XII, 18) That nothing be lacking to it: so also in the Church diverse persons to whom he has assigned diverse gifts.

*But if all were one,* not only would the multitude of the senses perish, but the body also. So if in the Church all were of one office and dignity, neither the members nor the body would be distinguished.

*Or again the head to the feet.* Dignity itself is contemptible without subjects. For office is that whereby dignity stands. A great emperor has need of an army.

VERS 23.-- *They are uncomely.* Far be it that there should be any foulness in the members of the saints: but they are called uncomely, because they have not that beauty of comeliness which those have that are in open view. Or on account of the law of the members which comes from sin; the unlawful use of the members is base, not the members themselves. There are understood also certain brethren who, though they are comely in poverty and in habit, are nevertheless sometimes of a cleaner life. *honesti*; read *inhonesti*, "unseemly" — the same gloss prints *inhonesti* of the same men two lines below Or there are understood those who, being uncomely in the Church through some sin, are more abundantly helped by consolations and by prayers, that they may become comely.

*But our comely parts.* As if he should say: So too for the brethren in whom the comeliness of their converse has adorned their zeal for skill, there is nothing that should be added by us. *But God hath tempered.* That which hinders being removed, he sets down that which profits, namely, a tempering together.

*But unto the same one for another.* As if he said: Let the members be solicitous, that they may tend unto the same thing, that is, unto that of solicitude which is itself, that is, undifferentiated, so that it be not less for another than for oneself.

*And if one member suffer.* Concerning the members of the body this is not doubtful, because if the eye or the foot be seized by some sickness, the whole body suffers with it. So too it becomes us to suffer with our brethren if any adversity has arisen, and to rejoice if it has gone well.
*Of a member.* Either of Christ, or from me, by whose preaching you were instructed.

*And some indeed.* Here he determines concerning the gifts of God, which are the higher and which the lower. For concerning these the Corinthians thought that the lesser was the greater, and that the greater was the lesser. *First.* In dignity and in time, *apostles,* preaching in the stead of Christ and judges of all .

*Secondly prophets.* That is, revealing the mysteries of the Scriptures or things to come. *Thirdly doctors.* Giving precepts of living, or who instruct boys in letters.

*Kinds of tongues. ((CHRYS.))* Behold, it is a gift of God, to know many tongues. And note that he puts last that which they put first.
*Are all prophets,* etc. He who has not these things in himself, let him love them in others: and in them he now has these things which he has not in himself.

*A more excellent way.* Charity, because it is a gift greater than all the aforesaid; whence at the end, to those who say, *Lord, in thy name we have prophesied, we have cast out devils, we have wrought miracles, the Lord shall say: Depart from me, I know you not, workers of iniquity* ((Matth. VII)).

notes.text: Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit — Being more abundantly strengthened after his conflict.
Being glorified of all — So God usually gives strong cordials after strong temptations. But neither their approbation continued long, nor the outward calm which he now enjoyed.

He stood up — Showing thereby that he had a desire to read the Scripture to the congregation: on which the book was given to him. It was the Jewish custom to read standing, but to preach sitting. Matt. xiii, 54; Mark vi, 1.
He found — It seems, opening upon it, by the particular providence of God.

He hath anointed me — With the Spirit. He hath by the power of his Spirit which dwelleth in me, set me apart for these offices. To preach the Gospel to the poor - Literally and spiritually. How is the doctrine of the ever-blessed trinity interwoven, even in those scriptures where one would least expect it? How clear a declaration of the great Three-One is there in those very words, The Spirit - of the Lord is upon me! To proclaim deliverance to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised - Here is a beautiful gradation, in comparing the spiritual state of men to the miserable state of those captives, who are not only cast into prison, but, like Zedekiah, had their eyes put out, and were laden and bruised with chains of iron. Isaiah lxi, 1.
The acceptable year — Plainly alluding to the year of jubilee, when all, both debtors and servants, were set free.
Today is this scripture fulfilled in your ears — By what you hear me speak.

glossa.text: *And the fame went out.* He is honoured not only by those present because of the miracles they had seen, but among the absent his fame was being spread abroad.
*He taught.* After the miracles, behold wisdom, by which he teaches, and by which teaching, through the preceding miracles, he magnifies.
*And he rose up to read. ((BEDA.))* He who had come not to be ministered unto but to minister, etc., *as far as* or he might correct them by the testimony of the reading of the prophecy.

*The Spirit. ((ID.))* In the earlier parts of the prophecy the Saviour, speaking of the calling of the Gentiles and the confirmation of the Church, etc., *as far as* because the Spirit of the Lord is upon him.

*To preach the gospel to the poor,* etc. He understands the Gentiles, who were truly poor. For they had neither the knowledge of God, nor the law, nor the prophets, nor anything else among their goods, and they were destitute of all the other spiritual riches.

*And when he had folded. ((BEDA.))* He read in the hearing of those who were present, etc., *as far as* but according to the capacity of the hearers he commits the word to the teacher to be dispensed.

lines: The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul.
Today this scripture is fulfilled in our hearing.
He has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.
Today this scripture is fulfilled in our hearing.
The joy of the Lord is your strength.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

Today this word is fulfilled in our hearing.
Good news to the poor, release to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the crushed.
Today this word is fulfilled in our hearing.
He rolls up the scroll and says: this is not someday; this is now, this is here.
Today this word is fulfilled in our hearing.
We are one body, joined to him and to each other; do not grieve, for the joy of the Lord is our strength.
Today this word is fulfilled in our hearing!
